messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I have a question on the theory of the SPDE approach constructing the Q matrix, it would be really great to get some help:

As stated in Result2, Lindgren et al 2011, the precision Q is Q = K*C^{-1}*K with K = kappa^2 C + G (for alpha = 2) and linear basis functions.  In INLA you have functionalities that do inference using the spde class on S^2 embedded in R^3 spaces. Following the method in Lindgren et al I was trying to construct the Q matrix on tetrahedral meshes in R^3. If I understand the theory correctly the formula would work for meshes in R^3 and the Q matrix would approximate the Matern field?..However, I found that the correlation matrix derived from the Q matrix (formula for alpha = 2) does not approximate the Matern field numerically..  I attached a toy example (sorry, the code is in Matlab). The codes contain a simple tetra mesh and the calculation of the tilde(C) and G matrices on the mesh. The result shows that the correlation matrix R has negative values..

Since I am quite sure about the calculation of the C and G matrices for tetrahedral meshes in R^3, I am wondering if I am missing something in the theory of the SPDE approach that causes the whole calculation in R^3 not approximating the Matern field (ie. the negative values in the corr matrix R)? Maybe you could give me some hints on what may be wrong here, and I have also few questions: Is the formula Q = K*C^{-1}*K with K = kappa^2 C + G (for alpha = 2) also correct for tetrahedral meshes in 3D?  In the proofs in Lindgren et al 2011, there are no restrictions on the dimension d, aren't there (I certainly do not understand everything)? Or does the tetrahedral mesh have to fulfill some restrictions, is the mesh in the toy example ill-conditioned?

Thank you very much for your help! I truly appreciate it!

Ran

messages.body_plain:
Hi,

it looks like your code is correct, and that it does generate the
correct exponential covariance that it should (with boundary effects of
course).
The issue you're seeing is that you example has an extremely low
resolution, so you're seeing mostly approximation errors.
I changed your code to use higher resolution:

d = (-5:5)/5;
[x,y,z] = meshgrid(d,d,d);  % A cube
x = [x(:)];
y = [y(:)];
z = [z(:)];

Then at the end I plotted the theoretical covariance function against
the numerical result, and got a very good match, considering that the
approximate range here is 2/kappa=2/3, which is close to the radius of
the domain (so the boundary effects are visible):

% Distances from the a reference point.  The origin is the furthest from
the boundary:
refpoint = [0,0,0]
% Identify the index of the reference point among the mesh coordinates
[tmp, refindex] = min(D);
% Assume that the reference point is a node in the mesh,
% and calculate distances:
D=sum((X-ones(size(X,1),1)*refpoint).^2,2).^0.5;

% Theoretical covariance, not taking boundary effects into account:
Dist = linspace(0,sqrt(3),200);
plot(Dist,1/(8*pi*kappa*tau^2).*exp(-kappa*Dist),'-')
% Add the numerical covariances:
hold on
plot(D,full(Cmat(refindex,:)),'o')
hold off

/Finn

For higher resolutions it's too expensive to calculate the whole
covariance matrix,but the covariance function for the reference point
can be obtained like this:

refind = zeros(size(X,1),1);
refind(refindex) = 1;
Cfun = Q\refind;

% Theoretical covariance, not taking boundary effects into account:
Dist = linspace(0,sqrt(3),200);
plot(Dist,1/(8*pi*kappa*tau^2).*exp(-kappa*Dist),'-')
% Add the numerical covariances:
hold on

plot(D,Cfun,'o')
hold off

/Finn

messages.subject: Integrating R-INLA code in a CRAN package (for outbreak detection)
messages.subject_clean: Integrating R-INLA code in a CRAN package (for outbreak detection)
messages.body_plain:
Dear R-INLA users and R-INLA maintainers,

just FYI a paper has just come out on how to use R-INLA to fit a Bayesian GAM as part of a outbreak detection algorithm.

http://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/bimj.201200141/abstract

Here is the abstract:
In infectious disease epidemiology, statistical methods are an indispensable component for the automated detection of outbreaks in routinely collected surveillance data. So far, methodology in this area has been largely of frequentist nature and has increasingly been taking inspiration from statistical process control. The present work is concerned with strengthening Bayesian thinking in this field. We extend the widely used approach of Farrington et al. and Heisterkamp et al. to a modern Bayesian framework within a time series decomposition context. This approach facilitates a direct calculation of the decision-making threshold while taking all sources of uncertainty in both prediction and estimation into account. More importantly, with the methodology it is now also possible to integrate covariate processes, e.g. weather influence, into the outbreak detection. Model inference is performed using fast and efficient integrated nested Laplace approximations, enabling the use of this method in routine surveillance at public health institutions. Performance of the algorithm was investigated by comparing simulations with existing methods as well as by analysing the time series of notified campylobacteriosis cases in Germany for the years 2002–2011, which include absolute humidity as a covariate process. Altogether, a flexible and modern surveillance algorithm is presented with an implementation available through the R package ‘surveillance’.

We are still trying to find a good way of integrating the R-INLA code (no CRAN availability) of the algorithm within a CRAN package. Anybody has any experiences with that?
We could of course just provide the files as downloads to source-in, but that does not appear to be a good solution.

Best regards,
Michael

#Load data from a shapefile included in the spdep package
